events.title: XMLHttpRequest introduced in IE5
events.summary: Microsoft shipped [XMLHttpRequest] with [Internet Explorer] 5 on March 18, 1999 — enabling JavaScript to fetch data without reloading the page.
events.about: XHR powered Gmail, Google Maps, and the AJAX revolution — `fetch()` and axios still solve the same problem. It turned browsers from document viewers into application runtimes that could talk to APIs asynchronously.

narrative.whyChosen: [XMLHttpRequest] enabled the first wave of rich web applications.
narrative.whyImportant: It made single-page interaction patterns possible before WebSockets.
narrative.problemSolved: Every user action required a full page reload to get new server data.

events.title: MQTT invented
events.summary: Andy Stanford-Clark and Arlen Nipper created MQTT v1 on March 26, 1999 — a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol for unreliable satellite links.
events.about: MQTT sends small messages between devices with minimal overhead — ideal for [IoT] sensors, industrial SCADA, and mobile networks. Brokers route topics like `factory/line1/temperature`; clients subscribe and publish with at-most-once or guaranteed delivery. AWS [IoT] Core, HiveMQ, and millions of embedded devices use it today.

narrative.whyChosen: MQTT solved messaging over expensive, high-latency satellite links for oil-pipeline monitoring.
narrative.whyImportant: It became the dominant wire protocol for [IoT] and constrained devices worldwide.
narrative.problemSolved: Heavy enterprise messaging protocols consumed too much bandwidth and battery for remote sensors.

events.title: Melissa macro virus spreads via email
events.summary: The Melissa virus began spreading on March 26, 1999 — a Word macro worm that emailed itself to the first 50 contacts in Microsoft Outlook address books.
events.about: Melissa overloaded corporate Exchange servers worldwide within days — the first mass-mailer worm to exploit email as its primary vector. It forced [IT] departments to disable Office macros by default and preview the phishing era: social engineering plus automation beats exotic exploits.

narrative.whyChosen: Melissa was the wake-up call that email could weaponize address books at scale.
narrative.whyImportant: It made macro security and mail filtering mandatory in enterprise [IT].
narrative.problemSolved: Nothing was solved initially — it showed Office macros plus Outlook were a self-propagating malware platform.
